No, that's not right. A language model doesn't remember earlier conversations on its own, so your assistant won't recall last week's chat unless you build that in.

It's an easy mistake to make. Chatbots like ChatGPT seem to remember because the app around the model re-sends the earlier messages with each new one. The model only ever sees the text in the request in front of it. When a session ends, nothing is kept inside the model, and a brand-new session starts blank.

Here's an example for your makerspace. Say a student tells the assistant on Monday, "I finished the laser cutter safety training." If you do nothing else, on the next Monday the model has no idea. To make it "remember", your code has to do two things:

1. **Save:** store that fact outside the model, for example as a row in a JSON file or database keyed by student.
2. **Load:** at the start of the next visit, look up that student's record and put the relevant facts into the prompt.

The model then seems to remember, but really it's reading what your code gave it.

This links to your mission goal of deciding what the assistant keeps in its context and what it saves between sessions. Two limits matter. The model only sees what fits in the prompt, and every token you load costs money. So you'll want to save a few key facts per student, like training status, and not whole transcripts.

Quick check: if a student says on Monday that they're certified on the 3D printer, and on Friday the assistant's prompt doesn't contain that fact, what would it answer when asked "Can I book the printer?" And what in your own code would fix that?

If you'd like, I can turn this into a short lesson on context and memory. It's the next topic in your plan.
